opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the thing that was really driving our thinking was that a lot of the benchmarks that existed at the time weren't telling us what we actually wanted to know. They'd be things like multiple-choice question sets, or very short, self-contained coding puzzles. Models would go from near zero to near saturation on them really quickly, and once they were saturated you'd learn almost nothing. You also didn't get a good sense of what a given score meant for the real world. If a model gets 80% on some exam-style benchmark, what does that tell you about whether it can actually do a meaningful chunk of a software engineer's job, or run an experiment end to end? Not much.

So when we put together the request for proposals, a few things were really central for me.

First, realism. We wanted tasks that look like the work people actually do, especially in domains that matter for the trajectory of AI, like software engineering, ML research engineering, cybersecurity, and science more broadly. They shouldn't be toy problems where the answer fits in a sentence. The agent should be in an environment with tools, a codebase, a terminal, maybe the internet, and it should have to figure out what to do.

Second, difficulty that spans a really wide range. One of my biggest frustrations was benchmarks that are all roughly the same difficulty, because then you get this sharp jump from "can't do any of it" to "can do all of it," and you can't see the trend. I wanted benchmarks with tasks ranging from things a skilled human could do in a few minutes all the way up to things that would take a skilled human days or weeks. That way you can actually track progress continuously and extrapolate, and it won't be immediately saturated by the next model generation.

Related to that, I was very interested in grounding difficulty in human terms. If you can say "this task takes a competent professional about eight hours," that's a much more meaningful unit than some abstract score. It lets you talk about how long a task can be before the AI starts to fail, and how that's changing over time. That's the kind of quantity you can reason about for forecasting and policy.

Third, we cared a lot about the benchmark being genuinely informative about risk-relevant capabilities. The question isn't just "is this model better than the last one," it's "is this model getting close to being able to substitute for a human researcher, or to autonomously do things that would be concerning?" So we wanted benchmarks where, if a model crossed a certain level, people would actually update and say "okay, this matters."

And then there's a bunch of practical stuff that ends up being really important: making sure the tasks aren't contaminated in training data, having reliable automated scoring where possible but not oversimplifying the task just to make it easy to grade, and making sure the elicitation is good, so you're giving the agent a reasonable scaffold and enough compute that you're measuring what the model can really do, not just what a lazy setup gets out of it. Underestimating capabilities is its own kind of risk.

So the ideal I had in my head was something like: if a lab released a new model tomorrow and I saw its score on this benchmark, I'd have a much clearer picture of what it could actually go do in the world, and roughly how far we are from the capability levels I'm worried about. Most benchmarks weren't giving us that, and that was the gap we were trying to fill.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts exam-style or short, self-contained model benchmarks with tasks where an agent works in a tool-equipped environment, identifying agent performance as the intended focus.

r002.rationale: The response calls for tasks spanning a wide difficulty range and avoiding rapid saturation, but does not say designers should suspect tasks are insufficiently difficult even when they believe the tasks are hard enough.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we were putting together that RFP, the thing I kept coming back to is that most existing benchmarks were measuring something pretty narrow. You'd have a bunch of self-contained tasks, each one maybe a few minutes long, with a clean success criterion, and the model either gets it or doesn't. That's useful, but it doesn't tell you much about the question I actually care about, which is: how close are these systems to being able to do substantial chunks of real economically valuable work, or substantial chunks of AI research itself, autonomously?

So the first property I wanted was that the tasks should be long. Not in the sense of a lot of tokens, but in the sense of a lot of sequential steps where you have to keep track of state, notice when something has gone wrong, and recover. A human expert might take hours or days to do them. That's where agents were falling down at the time, and it's where I expected the interesting action to be, because it's the dimension that separates "impressive demo" from "this thing can replace a contractor."

The second thing was that the tasks should be realistic, meaning they resemble work people actually get paid to do rather than puzzles invented for the benchmark. Puzzles are easy to construct and easy to grade, but they're also easy to overfit, and they don't give you a good read on the messy, under-specified nature of real tasks. I wanted things like: here's a codebase and a vague feature request, go figure out what's actually being asked and implement it. Or here's a research question and some data, produce something a domain expert would find credible.

Third, and this is the part people underrate, I wanted the benchmark to have a lot of headroom and to be graded in a way that gives you a gradient rather than a cliff. If the best model scores two percent and the next one scores three percent, that's not very informative. You want a distribution of task difficulties so that as models improve you can see the frontier moving, and ideally you want partial credit that reflects how far along the task the agent got before it fell apart. That lets you draw trend lines, which is really the whole point from a forecasting perspective.

And then the fourth thing, which is a practical constraint that ends up shaping everything, is that it has to be hard to contaminate. If the tasks are already on the internet, or if they're easy to memorize, the benchmark decays fast. So we were asking for either held-out tasks or tasks constructed in a way where memorization doesn't help you much, because the environment or the data is procedurally varied.

If I'm honest, there's a tension between all of these. Realistic long-horizon tasks are expensive to build and expensive to grade, often requiring human experts to evaluate the output. Partial credit is hard to define rigorously for open-ended work. So part of what the RFP was doing was saying: we know this is costly and awkward, we're willing to fund the costly and awkward version, because the cheap version isn't answering the question we need answered.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on agents doing long, realistic work but does not distinguish agent evaluation from chatbot model evaluation.

r002.rationale: It calls for headroom and varied task difficulty, but does not say designers should suspect tasks are still too easy even when they believe they are hard enough.

astra-6.text:
The thing I most wanted to understand was: can an AI system take a fairly big, messy task and actually get it done? A lot of benchmarks give the model a very neatly specified question, and then you evaluate its answer. But with an agent, a lot of what you care about is whether it can figure out what to do next, notice when something hasn’t worked, and recover without a human stepping in.

So I was excited about tasks that would take a human a substantial amount of time, where there’s some objective way to tell whether the work succeeded. It could be a coding task or a research task—the important thing is that you’re evaluating the whole process, rather than one little step that someone has already isolated for the model.

And you’d want a good human baseline. If you tell me an AI got 30 percent on a benchmark, that’s hard to interpret. If you tell me these are tasks that a person with a certain level of expertise can reliably complete in a few hours, that gives me a much better sense of what the AI can do. Especially if you can also tell me how much human help it needed along the way.

r001.rationale: It contrasts evaluating a model’s answer to a neatly specified question with evaluating an agent’s ability to manage and recover through a whole task.

r002.rationale: It recommends substantial tasks and a human baseline, but does not say designers should suspect their tasks are still insufficiently difficult even when they believe they are hard enough.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central thing we wanted was a benchmark where doing well would actually tell us something about an AI’s ability to carry out consequential tasks in the real world. There’s a big difference between answering a question that takes a human a few minutes and completing a project that takes someone several days, where you have to make a plan, notice when something isn’t working, and try a different approach.

So one thing I was excited about was tasks that vary in how long they take a human to complete. If we can see systems progressing from tasks that take a few minutes to tasks that take hours or days, that gives us a more interpretable picture of what’s changing.

And you want the evaluation to be realistic about what the system gets access to. Can it use tools? Can it get feedback from the environment? How much help does a human have to provide? Ideally, you’d have a clear way to check whether it accomplished the task, without having to prescribe every step along the way. The point is to measure whether it can get something done, including handling the messy parts, rather than whether it can produce something that looks like a good plan.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI systems carrying out consequential tasks, but never contrasts agent evaluation with chatbot model evaluation or identifies agents as the intended focus over chatbots.

r002.rationale: It calls for tasks ranging from minutes to hours or days, but does not say benchmark designers should suspect their tasks are still too easy even when they believe they are difficult.
